name: Beef organ / beef juice extract
lead: Beef organ and beef juice or meat extract supplements are concentrated products derived from cattle meat or offal, sold as nutrient-dense foods or capsules for muscle and general health. Offal means the internal organs of a butchered animal, and these are eaten in many cuisines [1]. Meat extract is a concentrated stock, first developed commercially in the nineteenth century [2].

No published trial reviewed here tests a branded organ or beef-juice capsule for muscle or appearance outcomes. A small registered study has examined the absorption and muscle-stimulating effect of hydrolysed minced beef [3]. Evidence for the supplement category is therefore thin.

paras: German chemist Justus von Liebig developed a concentrated beef extract in 1840, believing meat juices held nutrients lost in boiling; about 30 kg of meat made 1 kg of extract, which made it expensive [2]. Liebig's company opened a factory in Fray Bentos, Uruguay in 1865, and John Lawson Johnston created Bovril in the 1870s [2]. Today meat extract is mainly a flavouring [2].

Attitudes to offal vary: some cultures treat it as taboo while others eat it daily or as a delicacy [1]. In Ireland, Wikipedia reports consumption has risen with growing awareness of nutritional benefits, partly promoted by fitness influencers [1].

A small registered study (about 10 participants) examined absorption and muscle-stimulating effects of hydrolysed and minced beef; its status is listed as unknown and no results are summarised here [3]. Other registered trials examine ground beef or beef intake in contexts such as cardiovascular risk and ageing muscle [4], but these concern whole beef rather than organ or juice supplements. Laboratory studies from the 1970s and 1980s reported mutagenic compounds forming in cooked beef and beef extract and carcinogenicity of one such compound in mice [5]; their relevance to supplements is not established in these sources.

timeline.event: Liebig's company opens Fray Bentos factory in Uruguay [2]

card.summary: Concentrated beef organ or meat-juice products marketed as nutrient-dense muscle support; product-specific human evidence is thin.
card.aka: Beef liver/organ capsules, meat extract, beef juice
card.note: No trials of branded organ or juice supplements for appearance outcomes were found.

quick.overview:
These are products made from beef organs or concentrated beef extract, sold as nutrient-dense supplements. Meat extract dates to Liebig in 1840.

Offal is a traditional food in many cuisines. Studies of organ or juice supplements for muscle are essentially absent; related work covers beef protein in general.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that concentrated meat protein and micronutrients support muscle and general health. A small registered study looked at hydrolysed beef absorption.
quick.risks: Sold as food or supplement. Older lab studies found mutagenic compounds forming in cooked beef and beef extract; relevance to modern products is not established.
